title: Burning USDS refills the mint rate limit, making it a net-exposure cap rather than a throughput cap
content:
A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.5.2.1.2.2 specifies that a USDS burn is limited by `LIMIT_USDS_BURN`, and adds a coupling that is easy to overlook: "The burn additionally increases the `LIMIT_USDS_MINT` rate limit by the same amount, where that rate limit is configured, restoring minting capacity."

That one clause changes what the mint limit means. Without it, `LIMIT_USDS_MINT` would cap cumulative gross minting over the limit's window, and ordinary operational churn — mint, deploy, unwind, return — would burn through the allowance even though outstanding exposure never grew. With it, the limit tracks *net* issuance: only USDS that stays out consumes capacity.

This is the correct alignment for a risk control whose real subject is outstanding exposure rather than transaction volume, and it is why an Agent can operate continuously against a limit sized to its mandate instead of to its expected activity level.

The hedge matters too. Restoration happens only "where that rate limit is configured," so the refund is a property of a provisioned limit pair, not an unconditional accounting identity. The residual risk is that netting removes any bound on gross flow — an Agent can cycle arbitrarily large volumes through the vault so long as it returns them, so volume-sensitive concerns need a different control.
description: A burn increases LIMIT_USDS_MINT by the same amount where that limit is configured, so round-tripping does not exhaust minting capacity but net new issuance still does.
